debate.situation: You say most of your friends are buying homes or getting married, and you feel behind even though you are not sure you want those things. What you have reported is the feeling and the doubt; the reasons behind either are interpretations still to be examined. The decisive unknown is what the feeling is attached to: the milestones themselves, the friendships they may change, or a real deadline such as money or having children.

minds.title: The Imitation Detective
minds.concern: Whether a want, or the sense of lack, was borrowed from the people we watch.
minds.author: René Girard

minds.title: The Field Tester
minds.concern: Learning what you want by trying small, reversible things rather than by thinking harder.
minds.author: Herminia Ibarra

minds.title: The Defender of Odd Lives
minds.concern: Protecting your right to choose by your own judgment rather than by custom, while owning the cost.
minds.author: John Stuart Mill

debate.speaker: The Imitation Detective
debate.text: Start with the odd part: you feel behind on things you may not want. A race needs rivals. I suspect the milestones are lending you a scoreboard, and the scoreboard, not the house or the wedding, is what stings.
debate.author: René Girard
debate.basis: Basis: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel

debate.speaker: The Field Tester
debate.text: That is a theory about their head, and you cannot think your way to certainty. Not sure I want it might just mean untested. I would stop analyzing and run cheap experiments. Wanting is learned by doing small versions of the thing.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Defender of Odd Lives
debate.text: You both assume the doubt needs fixing. Perhaps this person simply wants a different life. Custom is not a reason. I would say that mankind needs different "experiments of living", and a person who copies the crowd uses only one faculty: imitation.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill
debate.basis: Basis: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty

debate.speaker: The Imitation Detective
debate.text: Fair hit on one point. Rebelling is also imitation, just with the sign flipped, so doubting the milestones proves nothing about independence. But notice what I did not claim: that you want these things. I claimed the feeling of lag needs a rival to exist.
debate.author: René Girard
debate.basis: Basis: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel

debate.speaker: The Field Tester
debate.text: Then list the rivals honestly, because the feeling could mean several things. Envy of their status. Loneliness as their weekends fill with partners and mortgages. Or a real clock, like wanting children or a financial window. Each needs a different response.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Defender of Odd Lives
debate.text: And the clock is the missing fact. If a real deadline exists, drifting is a choice with a price. If not, the pressure is purely social, and I would let it ring unanswered. I would add that my book defends your freedom to choose, not a guarantee that it costs nothing.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill
debate.basis: Basis: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty

debate.speaker: The Imitation Detective
debate.text: I doubt loneliness is likelier than envy. People often call it missing friends when the sharper pain is being ranked. But I will grant that if friendship is the wound, no scoreboard analysis helps. Different cause, different cure.
debate.author: René Girard
debate.basis: Basis: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel

debate.speaker: The Field Tester
debate.text: Blunt version: ranking motives from here is guesswork. Also, Mill, your odd life can be a hiding place. Never testing anything is not independence, it is avoidance with good branding.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Defender of Odd Lives
debate.text: Accepted, but I would narrow your tests. Do not date seriously just to collect data, or tour houses to feel normal. An experiment forced by the crowd is custom wearing a lab coat. Choose trials that fit this person's own aims, even if they point somewhere unusual.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill
debate.basis: Basis: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty

debate.speaker: The Field Tester
debate.text: Agreed, with a revision: test pieces, not packages. Ask married friends what they would keep and drop. Try a year of different living arrangements. Spend time on a project you would choose even if nobody saw. Cheap, reversible, informative.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Imitation Detective
debate.text: One conflict nobody has named: staying free and staying close to friends may pull apart. Which matters more is not mine to rank. And I would go further than my source here: ask whose approval you imagine when you feel behind.
debate.author: René Girard
debate.basis: Basis: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel

debate.clearer: The main insight is that feeling behind and wanting the milestones are separate questions: the feeling may come from a borrowed scoreboard, from changing friendships, or from a real deadline, and each reading points somewhere different. Still disputed is which of those is likeliest, and whether small tests are wise or merely another way of following the crowd. One possible self-reflection: when the feeling is strongest, who is the imagined audience, and does anything change if that person disappears?
debate.dependsOn: If a real deadline exists (for example wanting children, or a financial window) → small, early, reversible tests become more reasonable, because drifting has a cost you can name. If the feeling mostly appears around particular friends or events → the issue may be closeness or comparison rather than milestones, so repairing friendship or limiting comparison may help more than any test. If neither holds and the pressure is purely social → waiting or doing less is a serious option, because nothing is being lost while you stay unsure. If you do not know which applies → a proportionate way to learn is to notice, over a few weeks, when the feeling spikes and what it attaches to, and to try one or two low-cost pieces such as asking friends what they would keep and drop.
